terms.meaning: A shared place in the app where task data is kept and changed, so every screen sees the same tasks.
Settings a parent component passes into a component, like labels handed to a form field.
A smaller step inside a task that can be ticked off separately.
A countdown the app starts to help the user work on one task for its estimated time.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and setup
sections.what: Brings in the icons, the task and status types, the shared store, the badge component and the create or edit window. The first line marks the file as running in the browser.
sections.why: Likely reason: the card handles clicks and keeps local state, so it must run in the browser.
sections.watch_out: Several imported icons do not appear anywhere in this file, so they may be leftovers.

sections.name: TaskItemProps
sections.title: Inputs this card accepts
sections.what: Lists what the parent must provide: the task itself, plus optional flags for whether it is selected and a handler for selection changes.
sections.why: Likely reason: the same card is reused on several screens, and each screen passes only what it has.
sections.watch_out: The selection settings are optional, so a parent that omits them gets a card with no checkbox and no error.

sections.name: TaskItem (part 1)
sections.title: Store links, local state and card frame
sections.what: Connects the card to the store for status changes, deletes, focus timers and subtask ticks. Keeps local state for whether the edit window is open and whether subtasks are expanded. Draws the outer card and highlights it when selected.
sections.why: Likely reason: the store holds the real task data, so the card reads actions from it rather than keeping its own copy.
sections.watch_out: The status label table is defined here but does not appear in the rest of this file, so editing it may change nothing on screen.

sections.name: TaskItem (part 2)
sections.title: Status pill and title block
sections.what: Shows a colored status pill that is also a dropdown for changing status. Next to it shows the title, which gets a line through it when completed or cancelled, the priority badge, the category tag, and a one-line description.
sections.why: Likely reason: the status dropdown sits on the card so status can be changed without opening the edit window.
sections.watch_out: Mouse-down on the dropdown stops propagating, which keeps a drag from starting when the user picks a status on a draggable card.

sections.name: TaskItem (part 3)
sections.title: Action buttons and subtask checklist
sections.what: Adds a focus timer button that uses the task's estimate, an edit button that opens the create or edit window filled in with this task, and a delete button. When the task has subtasks, it adds a toggle that shows a checklist where each step can be ticked.
sections.why: Likely reason: common actions are kept on the card so a user can work from the list without visiting other screens.
sections.watch_out: The delete button removes the task at once, and nothing in the shown code asks the user to confirm.

summary: Shows one task as a card with controls to change its status, start a focus timer, edit it, delete it and tick off its subtasks.
purpose: Give the user a complete view of one task plus quick actions, so the same card can be reused in every task list.
why: Likely reason: keeping the card in one file means the list, board and table screens show a task the same way.
how: 1. Receives the task and optional selection settings from its parent screen. 2. Reads the actions it needs from the shared store. 3. Draws the colored status pill, which doubles as a status dropdown. 4. Draws the title, priority badge, category and one-line description. 5. Draws the focus timer, edit and delete buttons. 6. If the task has subtasks, draws a toggle that opens a checklist.
inputs: A task with an id, title, status, priority, category, description, time estimate and subtask list. Optional flags for selection and a selection handler from the parent.
outputs: A card on screen. Status changes, deletes, focus timer starts and subtask ticks go through the shared store. The edit window saves through the store as well.
risks: Delete happens immediately with no confirmation. Status and subtask changes save straight away, so a mistake is kept. Several imported icons, such as Tag and Zap, do not appear in the code.
debug: If a button does nothing, check the matching action in the store and confirm the task id is correct. If a status change does not stick, check the toggleTaskStatus action. If a subtask tick fails, check toggleSubtask. Try the same action on a newly created task to see if the problem is specific to one record.
